surfaces.part: top beam or cornice strip (tan, rows 1-2, cream wall below)
brown cap on the right pillar
cream wall with blue window (front face)
lavender-grey pillar strip and checkered dark panel on the right

answer.evidence: This is a tile-kit fragment of a wall with a window. Rows 1-2 at the top are a tan strip, and a brown strip sits over the right pillar. Neither has a front-edge line or eave shadow, and neither widens or narrows like an ellipse, so they read as a front-facing cornice. The silhouette is 13 wide from row 1 to row 15, with no roof slope or horizontal surface. The cream wall, blue window and lavender pillar below are all vertical faces. The result is a flat front elevation with at most a 2-row rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny object, about one tile, made of pale and blue panels. It is not a whole building: it has no roof, no wall mass and no door/window composition. The references are full houses with scalloped tile roofs, timber framing, plaster speckle and shaded stonework. The measured facts do not argue against this. The candidate has 15 visible tones in its tile, but only 15 distinct colours in the whole piece, against 185 and 66 for the references. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, but the piece is too small and simple to judge shading depth. It has only about 3 lightness steps per material and no per-tile or grain texture. It would look thinner and flatter than either reference, and it does not match the building kind.

answer.evidence: This is a flat, front-facing kit cell. Rows 1-2 are a thin tan cornice strip (L=168 then 204) that grades straight into the cream wall (L=250 from row 3). It has no front-edge line and no eave shadow, so it reads as a 1-2 row rim. Rows 3-15 are vertical faces: the cream wall with a blue window/door panel, and a gray pillar at x=11 (L=139) with a brown block at rows 1-2. The right-hand checkered strip is also drawn as a vertical face. No ellipse, roof plane or visible contents appear, and no receding side face is drawn. The silhouette is a constant 13 wide from row 1 to row 15, so no roof slope widens it.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate on the right of the magenta bar is a tiny sprite, about one tile in size. It looks like a blue and white window or panel, not a whole building. It has no roof with tile scallops, no wall mass and no door, so it does not match the building references. The measured facts (15 visible tones, 0% near-flat, 0% neutral dark edges) show a tinted outline and no large flat fills. However, the 15 tones are packed into a single tile-sized object. The references spread roof-tile highlights, plaster speckle and stone-by-stone shading over a much larger area. I see only about 3 shading steps on the candidate's main materials, against 5-6 on the references. A careful artist would not accept this next to the references as a building. When in doubt, fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny fragment, roughly 12x20 source pixels, that reads as a small blue and white window or door panel. It has no roof, no walls and no building mass, so it does not match the whole-building references (a tiled roof with timber-frame walls, and a stone-wall house). The measured facts are mildly favourable: 15 visible tones in its one tile against 10-12 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edges, which means the outline is tinted. These numbers come from a very small area, so they do not show equivalent richness. By eye it has only about 3 lightness steps on its blue and white areas.
